claim: RIPK1, RIPK3, ZBP1 and TRIF are the four mammalian proteins harboring RIP homotypic interaction motif (RHIM) domains.
source: RIPK1, RIPK3, ZBP1 and TRIF, the four mammalian proteins harboring RIP homotypic interaction motif (RHIM) domains, are key components of inflammatory signaling and programmed cell death.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual assertion about the composition of mammalian RHIM-domain proteins.

claim: RHIM-domain proteins are key components of inflammatory signaling and programmed cell death.
source: RIPK1, RIPK3, ZBP1 and TRIF, the four mammalian proteins harboring RIP homotypic interaction motif (RHIM) domains, are key components of inflammatory signaling and programmed cell death.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about the functional role of RHIM-domain proteins.

claim: RHIM-domain protein activation is mediated by their oligomerization.
source: RHIM-domain protein activation is mediated by their oligomerization; however, mechanisms that promote a return to homeostasis remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established mechanism.

claim: Mechanisms that promote a return to homeostasis of RHIM-domain proteins remain unknown.
source: RHIM-domain protein activation is mediated by their oligomerization; however, mechanisms that promote a return to homeostasis remain unknown.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract identifying a knowledge gap.

claim: Autophagy is critical for the turnover of all RHIM-domain proteins.
source: Here we show that autophagy is critical for the turnover of all RHIM-domain proteins.
evidence: This is the primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Macrophages lacking Atg16l1 accumulated highly insoluble forms of RIPK1, RIPK3, TRIF and ZBP1.
source: Macrophages lacking the autophagy gene Atg16l1accumulated highly insoluble forms of RIPK1, RIPK3, TRIF and ZBP1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunoblot data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Defective autophagy enhanced necroptosis by Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and Toll-like receptor (TLR) ligands.
source: Defective autophagy enhanced necroptosis by Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and Toll-like receptor (TLR) ligands.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell death assays in Figure 1.

claim: TNF-mediated necroptosis was mediated by RIPK1 kinase activity.
source: TNF-mediated necroptosis was mediated by RIPK1 kinase activity, whereas TLR3- or TLR4-mediated death was dependent on TRIF and RIPK3.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments using Necrostatin-1 (RIPK1 kinase inhibitor) in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: TLR3- or TLR4-mediated death was dependent on TRIF and RIPK3.
source: TNF-mediated necroptosis was mediated by RIPK1 kinase activity, whereas TLR3- or TLR4-mediated death was dependent on TRIF and RIPK3.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by CRISPR deletion experiments in Figure 2.

claim: Combined deletion of Atg16l1 and Zbp1 accelerated LPS-mediated necroptosis and sepsis in mice.
source: Unexpectedly, combined deletion of Atg16l1 and Zbp1 accelerated LPS-mediated necroptosis and sepsis in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro cell death assays (Figure 6) and in vivo sepsis experiments (Figure 7).

claim: ZBP1 drives necroptosis in the absence of the RIPK1-RHIM.
source: Thus, ZBP1 drives necroptosis in the absence of the RIPK1-RHIM, but suppresses this process when multiple RHIM-domain containing proteins accumulate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: ZBP1 suppresses necroptosis when multiple RHIM-domain containing proteins accumulate.
source: Thus, ZBP1 drives necroptosis in the absence of the RIPK1-RHIM, but suppresses this process when multiple RHIM-domain containing proteins accumulate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings, supported by data showing that Zbp1 deletion in Atg16l1-deficient cells enhanced necroptosis (Figure 6).

claim: Autophagy is a central regulator of innate inflammation governed by RHIM-domain proteins.
source: These findings identify autophagy as a central regulator of innate inflammation governed by RHIM-domain proteins.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the findings from the study.

claim: RIPK1 kinase activity drives caspase 8-dependent apoptosis.
source: Receptor interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) kinase activity drives caspase 8-dependent apoptosis as well as pro-inflammatory necroptosis dependent on RIPK3 and its substrate mixed lineage kinase domain like (MLKL) (Cho et al., 2009; He et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: RIPK1 kinase activity drives pro-inflammatory necroptosis dependent on RIPK3 and MLKL.
source: Receptor interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) kinase activity drives caspase 8-dependent apoptosis as well as pro-inflammatory necroptosis dependent on RIPK3 and its substrate mixed lineage kinase domain like (MLKL) (Cho et al., 2009; He et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: TRIF and ZBP1 can directly interact with RIPK1 and/or RIPK3 via their RHIM domains.
source: Additionally, the cytosolic adaptor Toll/IL-1 receptor (TIR) domain-containing adaptor protein inducing interferon−β (TRIF) and innate sensor Z-DNA binding protein 1 (ZBP1) can directly interact with RIPK1 and/or RIPK3 via their RHIM domains, thereby stabilizing downstream signaling (He et al., 2011; Kaiser et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2016; Newton et al., 2016; Thapa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: TRIF and ZBP1 stabilize downstream signaling by interacting with RIPK1 and/or RIPK3 via RHIM domains.
source: Additionally, the cytosolic adaptor Toll/IL-1 receptor (TIR) domain-containing adaptor protein inducing interferon−β (TRIF) and innate sensor Z-DNA binding protein 1 (ZBP1) can directly interact with RIPK1 and/or RIPK3 via their RHIM domains, thereby stabilizing downstream signaling (He et al., 2011; Kaiser et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2016; Newton et al., 2016; Thapa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: RHIM-dependent oligomerization of TRIF, RIPK1, RIPK3 and ZBP1 is required for their function.
source: RHIM-dependent oligomerization of TRIF, RIPK1, RIPK3 and ZBP1 is required for their function, but this also results in the generation of amyloid-like structures which require regulated turnover to prevent signal amplification (Kaiser et al., 2013; Li et al., 2012; Rebsamen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: RHIM-dependent oligomerization results in the generation of amyloid-like structures which require regulated turnover to prevent signal amplification.
source: RHIM-dependent oligomerization of TRIF, RIPK1, RIPK3 and ZBP1 is required for their function, but this also results in the generation of amyloid-like structures which require regulated turnover to prevent signal amplification (Kaiser et al., 2013; Li et al., 2012; Rebsamen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Selective autophagy targets the autophagic machinery to specific cargo via autophagy receptors.
source: Selective autophagy targets the autophagic machinery to specific cargo via autophagy receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about autophagy mechanisms.

claim: Forms of selective autophagy have been identified in the turnover of organelles, cytosolic pathogens and protein aggregates.
source: Forms of selective autophagy have been identified in the turnover of organelles, cytosolic pathogens and protein aggregates, ultimately driving their turnover via lysosomal degradation (Anding and Baehrecke, 2017; Khaminets et al., 2016; Levine et al., 2011; Mizushima, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Selective autophagy drives turnover of cargo via lysosomal degradation.
source: Forms of selective autophagy have been identified in the turnover of organelles, cytosolic pathogens and protein aggregates, ultimately driving their turnover via lysosomal degradation (Anding and Baehrecke, 2017; Khaminets et al., 2016; Levine et al., 2011; Mizushima, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient BMDMs were more sensitive than wild-type BMDMs to TNF plus zVAD-fmk-induced necroptosis.
source: Atg16l1 deficient bone marrow-derived macrophages (Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs) did not exhibit increased sensitivity to TNF alone, but they were more sensitive than wild-type (Atg16l1-WT) BMDMs to necroptotic stimulus of TNF plus pancaspase inhibitor zVAD-fmk (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient BMDMs did not exhibit increased sensitivity to TNF alone.
source: Atg16l1 deficient bone marrow-derived macrophages (Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs) did not exhibit increased sensitivity to TNF alone, but they were more sensitive than wild-type (Atg16l1-WT) BMDMs to necroptotic stimulus of TNF plus pancaspase inhibitor zVAD-fmk (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Necrostatin-1 reduced TNF/zVAD-induced death in both Atg16l1-WT and Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs.
source: Blocking the kinase activity of RIPK1 with Necrostatin-1 (Nec-1) reduced death in both Atg16l1-WT and Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs (Figure 1A), consistent with active RIPK1 engaging RIPK3 downstream of TNFR1 (Newton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Death induced by TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, TLR7/8 or TLR9 ligands plus zVAD-fmk was enhanced by Atg16l1 deficiency.
source: Death induced by TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, TLR7/8 or TLR9 ligands plus zVAD-fmk was also enhanced by Atg16l1 deficiency (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nec-1 was less effective at preventing TLR3- or TLR4-mediated death in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs compared with Atg16l1-WT BMDMs.
source: While Nec-1 suppressed necroptosis by TLR2, TLR7/8 and TLR9 ligands in both genotypes, it was less effective at preventing TLR3- or TLR4-mediated death in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs compared with Atg16l1-WT BMDMs (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IL-1β release by Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs was elevated upon LPS-mediated necroptosis independent of RIPK1 inhibition.
source: IL-1β release by Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs was also elevated upon LPS-mediated necroptosis independent of RIPK1 inhibition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Autocrine TNF production was elevated upon Atg16l1 deletion.
source: The modest effect of Nec-1 in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs may stem from it blocking necroptosis due to autocrine TNF production, which was elevated upon Atg16l1 deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), but not death due to other mechanisms activating RIPK3.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Deletion of Atg14l and Rb1cc1 significantly enhanced PolyI:C/zVAD- or LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis.
source: Deletion of Atg14l and Rb1cc1 significantly enhanced PolyI:C/zVAD- or LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis, whereas Rubcn deletion resulted in cell death levels comparable to Atg16l1-WT controls (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Rubcn deletion resulted in cell death levels comparable to Atg16l1-WT controls.
source: Deletion of Atg14l and Rb1cc1 significantly enhanced PolyI:C/zVAD- or LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis, whereas Rubcn deletion resulted in cell death levels comparable to Atg16l1-WT controls (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Atg14l and Rb1cc1-deficient BMDMs maintained elevated levels of cell death upon Nec-1 treatment.
source: As with loss of Atg16l1, Atg14l and Rb1cc1-deficient BMDMs maintained elevated levels of cell death upon Nec-1 treatment (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Canonical autophagy suppresses TLR3/4-induced necroptosis in BMDMs.
source: These results demonstrate that canonical autophagy suppresses TLR3/4-induced necroptosis in BMDMs and uncover a RIPK1 kinase-independent mode of cell death by TLR3/4 activation when autophagy is perturbed.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the genetic deletion experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: TLR3/4 activation induces a RIPK1 kinase-independent mode of cell death when autophagy is perturbed.
source: These results demonstrate that canonical autophagy suppresses TLR3/4-induced necroptosis in BMDMs and uncover a RIPK1 kinase-independent mode of cell death by TLR3/4 activation when autophagy is perturbed.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the genetic deletion experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Deletion of Ripk3 and Mlkl but not Gsdmd prevented LPS/zVAD- and TNF/zVAD-induced death in both Atg16l1-WT and Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs.
source: Deletion of Ripk3 and Mlkl but not Gsdmd prevented LPS/zVAD- and TNF/zVAD-induced death in both Atg16l1-WT and Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs, confirming that macrophage death was due to necroptosis (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Macrophage death induced by LPS/zVAD and TNF/zVAD was due to necroptosis.
source: Deletion of Ripk3 and Mlkl but not Gsdmd prevented LPS/zVAD- and TNF/zVAD-induced death in both Atg16l1-WT and Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs, confirming that macrophage death was due to necroptosis (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the genetic deletion experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Neither Nlrp3 nor Pycard knockdown prevented RIPK1 kinase-independent cell death in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs.
source: However, neither Nlrp3 nor Pycard knockdown prevented RIPK1 kinase-independent cell death in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Secondary pyroptosis does not contribute to the death of Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs treated with LPS/zVAD or PolyI:C/zVAD.
source: Therefore, secondary pyroptosis does not appear to contribute to the death of Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs treated with LPS/zVAD or PolyI:C/zVAD.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the Nlrp3 and Pycard knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Knockdown of Ticam1 in Atg16l1-WT or Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs decreased necroptosis induced by PolyI:C/zVAD or LPS/zVAD.
source: As expected, knockdown of Ticam1 (encoding TRIF) in Atg16l1-WT or Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs also decreased necroptosis induced by PolyI:C/zVAD or LPS/zVAD, although additional inhibition of RIPK1 provided a more complete rescue of cell death (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 2C, 2D, and 2E.

claim: Additional inhibition of RIPK1 provided a more complete rescue of cell death than Ticam1 knockdown alone.
source: As expected, knockdown of Ticam1 (encoding TRIF) in Atg16l1-WT or Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs also decreased necroptosis induced by PolyI:C/zVAD or LPS/zVAD, although additional inhibition of RIPK1 provided a more complete rescue of cell death (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 2C, 2D, and 2E.

claim: TNFR2-Fc attenuated necroptosis of Atg16l1-WT BMDMs comparably to Nec-1.
source: TNFR2-Fc attenuated necroptosis of Atg16l1-WT BMDMs comparably to Nec-1, especially with TLR2 or TLR9 ligands or TNF itself (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,E,F), but also with TLR3, TLR4 or TLR7 ligands (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TNFR2-Fc failed to inhibit necroptosis in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs treated with TLR2, TLR7 or TLR9 ligands.
source: In contrast, TNFR2-Fc failed to inhibit necroptosis in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs treated with TLR2, TLR7 or TLR9 ligands (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,D,E), despite inhibiting necroptosis induced by TLR3 or TLR4 ligands or TNF comparably to Nec-1 (TNFR2-Fc, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C, F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TNF contributes to enhanced necroptosis of Atg16l1-deficient BMDMs.
source: Thus, while TNF contributes to enhanced necroptosis of Atg16l1-deficient BMDMs, activation of RIPK1 contributes more to this phenotype, perhaps indicating the involvement of multiple death receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the TNFR2-Fc blocking experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of IFNAR1 prevented TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, or TLR9-induced necroptosis in Atg16l1-WT BMDMs.
source: Consistent with the results of McComb et al. (2014), pharmacological blockade of IFNAR1 prevented TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, or TLR9-induced necroptosis in Atg16l1-WT BMDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B,C,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: IFNAR1 blockade decreased TLR3- or TLR4-induced necroptosis of Atg16l1-deficient BMDMs more than Nec-1.
source: IFNAR1 blockade also decreased TLR3- or TLR4-induced necroptosis of Atg16l1-deficient BMDMs more than Nec-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and 2C.

claim: Phosphorylation of STAT1 was increased in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs following LPS/zVAD treatment.
source: Accordingly, phosphorylation of STAT1, which is associated with Type I interferon signaling, was increased in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs following LPS/zVAD treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Type I interferon signaling contributes to enhanced necroptosis of Atg16l1-deficient BMDMs, particularly with ligands that activate TRIF.
source: These data indicate that signaling by Type I interferons contributes to enhanced necroptosis of Atg16l1-deficient BMDMs, particularly with ligands that activate TRIF.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the IFNAR1 blocking experiments and STAT1 phosphorylation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TRIF appeared to be monomeric in untreated BMDMs of both genotypes.
source: TRIF appeared to be monomeric in untreated BMDMs of both genotypes, running as a single band in the detergent (NP-40) soluble fraction below the 100-kDa mark in an SDS-PAGE gel (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: LPS was sufficient to elicit a smear of NP40-insoluble, slower migrating TRIF species that was far more prominent in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs than in Atg16l1-WT BMDMs.
source: LPS was sufficient to elicit a smear of NP40-insoluble, slower migrating TRIF species that was far more prominent in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs than in Atg16l1-WT BMDMs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: High-MW species of autophosphorylated RIPK1 and total RIPK1 largely accumulated in the NP-40 insoluble fraction after treatment with LPS plus zVAD.
source: High-MW species of autophosphorylated RIPK1 (p-RIPK1, Ser166/Thr169) as well as total RIPK1 largely accumulated in the NP-40 insoluble fraction after treatment with LPS plus zVAD; these were more abundant in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs than in Atg16l1-WT BMDMs (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: High-MW species of autophosphorylated RIPK1 and total RIPK1 were more abundant in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs than in Atg16l1-WT BMDMs after LPS/zVAD treatment.
source: High-MW species of autophosphorylated RIPK1 (p-RIPK1, Ser166/Thr169) as well as total RIPK1 largely accumulated in the NP-40 insoluble fraction after treatment with LPS plus zVAD; these were more abundant in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs than in Atg16l1-WT BMDMs (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Slower migrating species of both autophosphorylated RIPK3 and total RIPK3 in the insoluble fraction after treatment with LPS plus zVAD were elevated in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs when compared with Atg16l1-WT BMDMs.
source: Slower migrating species of both autophosphorylated RIPK3 (Thr231/Ser232) and total RIPK3 in the insoluble fraction after treatment with LPS plus zVAD were also elevated in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs when compared with Atg16l1-WT BMDMs (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: Knockdown of Ticam1 decreased the amount of autophosphorylated RIPK3 and autophosphorylated RIPK1 in Atg16l1-cKO cells.
source: Knockdown of Ticam1 decreased the amount of autophosphorylated RIPK3 and autophosphorylated RIPK1 in Atg16l1-cKO cells (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D and 3F.

claim: Loss of Atg16l1 did not appear to affect the abundance of monomeric TRIF, RIPK1, or RIPK3 in the detergent soluble fraction.
source: Loss of Atg16l1 did not appear to affect the abundance of monomeric TRIF, RIPK1, or RIPK3 in the detergent soluble fraction (Figure 3A,C,E), suggesting that autophagic turnover specifically regulates levels of activated/modified forms of TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A, 3C, and 3E.

claim: Autophagic turnover specifically regulates levels of activated/modified forms of TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3.
source: Loss of Atg16l1 did not appear to affect the abundance of monomeric TRIF, RIPK1, or RIPK3 in the detergent soluble fraction (Figure 3A,C,E), suggesting that autophagic turnover specifically regulates levels of activated/modified forms of TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the immunoblot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs treated with LPS plus zVAD contained more MLKL phosphorylated at Ser345 when compared to wild-type counterparts.
source: Consistent with reduced autophagic turnover of RHIM proteins enhancing TLR4-induced necroptosis, Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs treated with LPS plus zVAD contained more MLKL phosphorylated at Ser345, a marker of necroptosis (Sun et al., 2012; Cai et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Dondelinger et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014), when compared to their wild-type counterparts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis killed more than 80% of Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs within 3 hr of treatment, compared to approximately 50% of Atg16l1-WT BMDMs.
source: Measuring the kinetics of cell death revealed that LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis killed more than 80% of Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs within 3 hr of treatment, compared to approximately 50% of Atg16l1-WT BMDMs (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by kinetic cell death data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Atg16l1-deficient BMDMs were more sensitive than Atg16l1-WT BMDMs to TLR3 engagement alone without zVAD.
source: Interestingly, Atg16l1-deficient BMDMs were more sensitive than Atg16l1-WT BMDMs to TLR3 engagement alone without zVAD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), consistent with TLR3 and TRIF having the capacity to assemble a death-inducing signaling complex that activates caspase-8 (Zinngrebe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: High-MW forms of TRIF accumulated transiently and with similar kinetics in both genotypes, peaking at 1 hr, and to a greater extent in the absence of Atg16l1.
source: We analyzed TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3 in the detergent-insoluble fraction in the first 6 hr after treatment with LPS/zVAD, and found that high-MW forms of TRIF accumulated transiently and with similar kinetics in both genotypes, peaking at 1 hr, and to a greater extent in the absence of Atg16l1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Accumulation of autophosphorylated, high-MW RIPK1 and RIPK3 peaked at 2 hr after LPS/zVAD treatment in both genotypes, with greater accumulation in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs.
source: Accumulation of autophosphorylated, high-MW RIPK1 and RIPK3 peaked at 2 hr after LPS/zVAD treatment in both genotypes, with greater accumulation in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Autophosphorylated RIPK1 and RIPK3 were ubiquitinated with Met1- or Lys63-linked chains, with greater abundance in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs.
source: Autophosphorylated RIPK1 and RIPK3 were also ubiquitinated with Met1- or Lys63-linked chains, with greater abundance in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Accumulation of ubiquitinated protein aggregates is a hallmark of defective autophagy.
source: Indeed, accumulation of ubiquitinated protein aggregates is a hallmark of defective autophagy (Kwon and Ciechanover, 2017; Dikic, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text with supporting citations.

claim: Treatment of WT BMDMs with Bafilomycin A1 resulted in accumulation of high-MW forms of TRIF and RIPK1 in detergent insoluble fractions during LPS/zVAD-mediated necroptosis over 6 hr.
source: Consistent with our genetic models, treatment of WT BMDMs with Bafilomycin A1, an inhibitor lysosomal vacuolar H-ATPases, resulted in accumulation of high-MW forms of TRIF and RIPK1 in detergent insoluble fractions during LPS/zVAD-mediated necroptosis over 6 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Basal turnover of low-MW TRIF, RIPK1, and RIPK3 was not perturbed in a reproducible manner by Bafilomycin A1.
source: In contrast, basal turnover of low-MW TRIF, RIPK1, and RIPK3 was not perturbed in a reproducible manner by Bafilomycin A1.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: Inhibition of proteasomal degradation with MG-132 caused a very subtle increase in low-MW TRIF and RIPK1, whereas RIPK3 appeared unaffected.
source: For comparison, inhibition of proteasomal degradation with MG-132 caused a very subtle increase in low-MW TRIF and RIPK1, whereas RIPK3 appeared unaffected Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: Lysosomal turnover via autophagy is critical for preventing the accumulation of active TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that lysosomal turnover via autophagy is critical for preventing the accumulation of active TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3, and its loss exacerbates necroptotic signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the genetic and pharmacological experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Loss of lysosomal turnover via autophagy exacerbates necroptotic signaling.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that lysosomal turnover via autophagy is critical for preventing the accumulation of active TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3, and its loss exacerbates necroptotic signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the genetic and pharmacological experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Treatment with LPS/zVAD in the presence of Bafilomycin A1 revealed accumulation of lipidated LC3B (LC3-II) in WT BMDMs.
source: Treatment with LPS/zVAD in the presence of Bafilomycin A1 to halt autophagic flux revealed accumulation of lipidated LC3B (LC3-II) in WT BMDMs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Levels of the autophagy receptors SQSTM1/p62, TAX1BP1 and CALCOCO1 were elevated upon Bafilomycin A1 treatment, especially in the detergent-insoluble fraction.
source: Levels of the autophagy receptors SQSTM1/p62, TAX1BP1 and CALCOCO1 were elevated upon Bafilomycin A1 treatment, especially in the detergent-insoluble fraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G and 2H.

claim: Autophagic flux was ongoing during necroptosis.
source: These data suggest that autophagic flux was ongoing during necroptosis and that autophagy receptors accumulated in the same subcellular compartment as active TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the LC3 and autophagy receptor data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G and 2H.

claim: Autophagy receptors accumulated in the same subcellular compartment as active TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3.
source: These data suggest that autophagic flux was ongoing during necroptosis and that autophagy receptors accumulated in the same subcellular compartment as active TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the autophagy receptor data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G and 2H.

claim: The selective autophagy receptor TAX1BP1 suppresses TRIF abundance and TRIF-dependent IFNβ production in BMDMs.
source: We and others have observed that the selective autophagy receptor TAX1BP1 suppresses TRIF abundance and TRIF-dependent IFNβ production in BMDMs (Samie et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text with supporting citations.

claim: SQSTM1/p62, TAX1BP1 and CALCOCO1 were identified as candidate selective autophagy receptors in BMDMs during TLR4 activation.
source: These findings are consistent with our unbiased proteomics-based identification of SQSTM1/p62, TAX1BP1 and CALCOCO1 as candidate selective autophagy receptors in BMDMs during TLR4 activation (Samie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a supporting citation.

claim: SQSTM1/p62, TAX1BP1 and CALCOCO1 accumulated with varying kinetics after treatment with LPS/zVAD.
source: Immunoblotting revealed accumulation of SQSTM1/p62, TAX1BP1 and CALCOCO1 with varying kinetics after treatment with LPS/zVAD, and loss of Atg16l1 further increased the levels of these receptors in the detergent-insoluble fraction (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Loss of Atg16l1 further increased the levels of SQSTM1/p62, TAX1BP1 and CALCOCO1 in the detergent-insoluble fraction.
source: Immunoblotting revealed accumulation of SQSTM1/p62, TAX1BP1 and CALCOCO1 with varying kinetics after treatment with LPS/zVAD, and loss of Atg16l1 further increased the levels of these receptors in the detergent-insoluble fraction (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Loss of Tax1bp1 enhanced BMDM death by either PolyI:C/zVAD or LPS/zVAD treatment.
source: Loss of Tax1bp1 enhanced BMDM death by either PolyI:C/zVAD or LPS/zVAD treatment. Necroptosis in both settings was only partially blocked by Nec-1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Necroptosis induced by PolyI:C/zVAD or LPS/zVAD in Tax1bp1-deficient BMDMs was only partially blocked by Nec-1.
source: Loss of Tax1bp1 enhanced BMDM death by either PolyI:C/zVAD or LPS/zVAD treatment. Necroptosis in both settings was only partially blocked by Nec-1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Knockdown of Sqstm1 or Calcoco1 did not increase TLR3- or TLR4-induced necroptosis in BMDMs.
source: In contrast, knockdown of Sqstm1 or Calcoco1 did not increase TLR3- or TLR4-induced necroptosis in BMDMs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The autophagy receptor TAX1BP1 suppresses BMDM necroptosis downstream of TRIF.
source: Thus, the autophagy receptor TAX1BP1 suppresses BMDM necroptosis downstream of TRIF.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the Tax1bp1 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ZBP1 was identified as one of the most highly accumulated proteins in Atg16l1-deficient macrophages.
source: We recently identified the RHIM-domain containing protein ZBP1 as one of the most highly accumulated proteins in Atg16l1-deficient macrophages (Samie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a supporting citation.

claim: Loss of Atg16l1 resulted in basal accumulation of ZBP1.
source: Loss of Atg16l1 resulted in basal accumulation of ZBP1 as shown by a cycloheximide-chase assay (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Basal turnover of ZBP1 was attenuated by lysosomal inhibition.
source: In contrast to TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3, basal turnover of ZBP1 was attenuated by lysosomal inhibition, because treatment with Bafilomycin A1, but not MG132, resulted in ZBP1 accumulation in WT BMDMs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with Bafilomycin A1, but not MG132, resulted in ZBP1 accumulation in WT BMDMs.
source: In contrast to TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3, basal turnover of ZBP1 was attenuated by lysosomal inhibition, because treatment with Bafilomycin A1, but not MG132, resulted in ZBP1 accumulation in WT BMDMs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ZBP1 accumulated during LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis, and this was enhanced by Atg16l1 deletion.
source: ZBP1 also accumulated during LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis, and this was enhanced by Atg16l1 deletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CRISPR-mediated deletion of Zbp1 in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs further enhanced LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis.
source: However, CRISPR-mediated deletion of Zbp1 in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs (Figure 6B) further enhanced LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis, and this death was prevented by deletion of Ticam1 but not by Nec-1 (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Death in Atg16l1-cKO; Zbp1-deleted BMDMs was prevented by deletion of Ticam1 but not by Nec-1.
source: However, CRISPR-mediated deletion of Zbp1 in Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs (Figure 6B) further enhanced LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis, and this death was prevented by deletion of Ticam1 but not by Nec-1 (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ZBP1 appears to suppress TRIF-mediated necroptosis.
source: Therefore, contrary to expectations, ZBP1 appears to suppress TRIF-mediated necroptosis (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the Zbp1 deletion experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Loss of Zbp1 did not impact the death of autophagy-sufficient BMDMs.
source: Notably, loss of Zbp1 did not impact the death of autophagy-sufficient BMDMs, suggesting that levels of ZBP1 must cross a certain threshold before suppressing TRIF-dependent necroptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the cell death data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Levels of ZBP1 must cross a certain threshold before suppressing TRIF-dependent necroptosis.
source: Notably, loss of Zbp1 did not impact the death of autophagy-sufficient BMDMs, suggesting that levels of ZBP1 must cross a certain threshold before suppressing TRIF-dependent necroptosis.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on the cell death data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: CRISPR-mediated deletion of Zbp1 alone did not impact cell death at any dose of LPS.
source: CRISPR-mediated deletion of Zbp1 alone did not impact cell death at any dose of LPS (Figure 6D), but combined with defective autophagy, Zbp1 deletion sensitized cells to necroptosis at low doses of LPS, even in the presence of Nec-1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Combined with defective autophagy, Zbp1 deletion sensitized cells to necroptosis at low doses of LPS, even in the presence of Nec-1.
source: CRISPR-mediated deletion of Zbp1 alone did not impact cell death at any dose of LPS (Figure 6D), but combined with defective autophagy, Zbp1 deletion sensitized cells to necroptosis at low doses of LPS, even in the presence of Nec-1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Overabundant ZBP1 can antagonize TRIF-mediated necroptosis in Atg16l1-deficient macrophages.
source: Thus, overabundant ZBP1 can antagonize TRIF-mediated necroptosis in Atg16l1-deficient macrophages.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the Zbp1 deletion experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Zbp1 deletion accelerated LPS/zVAD-mediated necroptosis of Atg16l1-deficient macrophages.
source: We confirmed our CRISPR-based observations by generating conditional-knockout mice lacking Atg16l1 (Atg16l1-cKO; Zbp1-WT) or Atg16l1 and Zbp1 (Atg16l1-cKO; Zbp1-cKO) in myeloid cells. Consistent with our earlier results, Zbp1 deletion accelerated LPS/zVAD-mediated necroptosis of Atg16l1-deficient macrophages (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ZBP1 deficiency did not affect the accumulation of TRIF in the detergent insoluble fraction of Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs treated with LPS/zVAD.
source: ZBP1 deficiency did not affect the accumulation of TRIF in the detergent insoluble fraction of Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs treated with LPS/zVAD (Figure 6F), arguing that ZBP1 interferes with signaling events further downstream.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: ZBP1 interferes with signaling events downstream of TRIF.
source: ZBP1 deficiency did not affect the accumulation of TRIF in the detergent insoluble fraction of Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs treated with LPS/zVAD (Figure 6F), arguing that ZBP1 interferes with signaling events further downstream.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on the immunoblot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: BMDMs lacking both Atg16l1 and Zbp1 contained more high MW species of autophosphorylated RIPK1 after treatment with LPS/zVAD compared to Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs.
source: Indeed, compared to Atg16l1-cKO BMBMs, BMDMs lacking both Atg16l1 and Zbp1 contained more high MW species of autophosphorylated RIPK1 (Figure 6G) and autophosphorylated RIPK3 (Figure 6H) after treatment with LPS/zVAD.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: BMDMs lacking both Atg16l1 and Zbp1 contained more high MW species of autophosphorylated RIPK3 after treatment with LPS/zVAD compared to Atg16l1-cKO BMDMs.
source: Indeed, compared to Atg16l1-cKO BMBMs, BMDMs lacking both Atg16l1 and Zbp1 contained more high MW species of autophosphorylated RIPK1 (Figure 6G) and autophosphorylated RIPK3 (Figure 6H) after treatment with LPS/zVAD.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Myeloid-specific loss of Atg16l1 sensitizes mice to LPS-mediated sepsis in vivo.
source: Beyond cellular necroptosis, myeloid-specific loss of Atg16l1 sensitizes mice to LPS-mediated sepsis in vivo (Samie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a supporting citation.

claim: Intraperitoneal administration of LPS reproduced the previously observed sensitization of Atg16l1-cKO mice.
source: Intraperitoneal administration of LPS (10 mg per kg body weight) reproduced the previously observed sensitization of Atg16l1-cKO mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Combined loss of Atg16l1 and Zbp1 significantly accelerated morbidity, with double-knockout mice succumbing to LPS-driven mortality by 14 hr.
source: Combined loss of Atg16l1 and Zbp1 significantly accelerated morbidity, with double-knockout mice succumbing to LPS-driven mortality by 14 hr.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Loss of Zbp1 alone did not impact morbidity in LPS-mediated sepsis.
source: Loss of Zbp1 alone did not impact morbidity (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Atg16l1 deficiency in myeloid cells exacerbated LPS-induced IL-1β and TNF in the serum.
source: Atg16l1 deficiency in myeloid cells exacerbated LPS-induced IL-1β and TNF in the serum, and the amount of IL-1β was yet higher in Atg16l1-cKO; Zbp1-cKO double-knockout mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The amount of IL-1β was higher in Atg16l1-cKO; Zbp1-cKO double-knockout mice compared to Atg16l1-cKO mice.
source: Atg16l1 deficiency in myeloid cells exacerbated LPS-induced IL-1β and TNF in the serum, and the amount of IL-1β was yet higher in Atg16l1-cKO; Zbp1-cKO double-knockout mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Autophagy regulates ZBP1 abundance in macrophages.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that: 1) autophagy regulates ZBP1 abundance in macrophages, 2) elevated ZBP1 suppresses necroptosis when autophagy is perturbed, and 3) loss of both Atg16l1 and Zbp1 in myeloid cells accelerates LPS-mediated inflammation, enhancing morbidity in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the findings shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Elevated ZBP1 suppresses necroptosis when autophagy is perturbed.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that: 1) autophagy regulates ZBP1 abundance in macrophages, 2) elevated ZBP1 suppresses necroptosis when autophagy is perturbed, and 3) loss of both Atg16l1 and Zbp1 in myeloid cells accelerates LPS-mediated inflammation, enhancing morbidity in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the findings shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Loss of both Atg16l1 and Zbp1 in myeloid cells accelerates LPS-mediated inflammation, enhancing morbidity in vivo.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that: 1) autophagy regulates ZBP1 abundance in macrophages, 2) elevated ZBP1 suppresses necroptosis when autophagy is perturbed, and 3) loss of both Atg16l1 and Zbp1 in myeloid cells accelerates LPS-mediated inflammation, enhancing morbidity in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the findings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Defective autophagy in macrophages leads to an accumulation of modified RIPK1, RIPK3, and TRIF in response to pro-inflammatory signals.
source: Here, we show that defective autophagy in macrophages leads to an accumulation of modified RIPK1, RIPK3, and TRIF in response to pro-inflammatory signals, precipitating inflammation and necroptosis in a stimulus-dependent manner (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Defective autophagy precipitates inflammation and necroptosis in a stimulus-dependent manner.
source: Here, we show that defective autophagy in macrophages leads to an accumulation of modified RIPK1, RIPK3, and TRIF in response to pro-inflammatory signals, precipitating inflammation and necroptosis in a stimulus-dependent manner (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: TRIF can promote RIPK1 kinase-independent, RIPK3-dependent necroptosis when its accumulation is not checked by autophagy.
source: Specifically, we noted that TRIF can promote RIPK1 kinase-independent, RIPK3-dependent necroptosis when its accumulation is not checked by autophagy.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the findings shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: TRIF can engage RIPK3 directly without the need for RIPK1.
source: TRIF can engage RIPK3 directly without the need for RIPK1 (Kaiser et al., 2013; Newton et al., 2016), so a scaffolding role for RIPK1 is unlikely.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: A scaffolding role for RIPK1 in TRIF-mediated necroptosis is unlikely.
source: TRIF can engage RIPK3 directly without the need for RIPK1 (Kaiser et al., 2013; Newton et al., 2016), so a scaffolding role for RIPK1 is unlikely.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion based on cited literature.

claim: ZBP1 contains multiple RHIM-domains that support formation of amyloid-like structures.
source: ZBP1 contains multiple RHIM-domains that support formation of amyloid-like structures (Li et al., 2012; Rebsamen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Accumulation of ZBP1 induced by defective autophagy may perturb optimal TRIF- or RIPK3- signaling via RHIM-mediated interference.
source: Accumulation of ZBP1 induced by defective autophagy may perturb optimal TRIF- or RIPK3- signaling via RHIM-mediated interference.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion based on the findings shown in Figure 6.

claim: RHIM-dependent stacking of RIPK1 and RIPK3 is a key feature of the necrosome.
source: In mammalian cells, RHIM-dependent stacking of RIPK1 and RIPK3 has been described as a key feature of the necrosome (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: RHIM-dependent accumulation of TRIF is a pre-requisite for TRIF-mediated inflammatory signaling.
source: RHIM-dependent accumulation of TRIF is also acknowledged as a pre-requisite for TRIF-mediated inflammatory signaling (Gentle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Biophysical characteristics of RHIM-domain protein complexes include a highly insoluble nature and resistance to denaturation/degradation.
source: Biophysical characteristics of RHIM-domain protein complexes include a highly insoluble nature and resistance to denaturation/degradation (Fowler et al., 2007; Kleino et al., 2017; Lamour et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Ubiquitination of cytosolic proteins is an established mechanism of substrate-identification by selective autophagy.
source: Ubiquitination of cytosolic proteins is an established mechanism of substrate-identification by selective autophagy, and TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3 are ubiquitinated during inflammatory signaling (Yang et al., 2017; Choi et al., 2018; de Almagro et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3 are ubiquitinated during inflammatory signaling.
source: Ubiquitination of cytosolic proteins is an established mechanism of substrate-identification by selective autophagy, and TRIF, RIPK1 and RIPK3 are ubiquitinated during inflammatory signaling (Yang et al., 2017; Choi et al., 2018; de Almagro et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Ubiquitinated RIPK1 and RIPK3 were more abundant after LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis when autophagy was compromised.
source: Although ubiquitinated RIPK1, and RIPK3 were more abundant after LPS/zVAD-induced necroptosis when autophagy was compromised, further investigation is needed to define the components of the selective autophagy machinery that drive the turnover of RHIM-domain proteins, and to determine whether ubiquitination is a critical step in this process.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Defects in autophagy promote inflammatory diseases such as Crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and neurodegeneration.
source: Genome-wide association (GWA) and functional studies have revealed that defects in autophagy promote inflammatory diseases such as Crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and neurodegeneration (Levine et al., 2011; Mizushima, 2007; Matsuzawa-Ishimoto et al., 2017; Samie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The findings provide a potential link between defective autophagy and necroptotic signaling.
source: Our findings provide a potential link between defective autophagy and necroptotic signaling, with autophagy promoting the turnover of RHIM-containing proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Autophagy promotes the turnover of RHIM-containing proteins.
source: Our findings provide a potential link between defective autophagy and necroptotic signaling, with autophagy promoting the turnover of RHIM-containing proteins.
